# 4 Maccabees Chapter 3 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Greek MS (Codex Sinaiticus) | **Section:** Historical Examples of Reason's Sovereignty

---

**1** I could bring forward many examples from Scripture to prove that reason governs the passions.

**2** When David was waging war against the Philistines, his army grew thirsty toward evening, and David longed intensely for water from a spring in enemy territory.

**3** Two brave soldiers, to please their king, armed themselves and slipped through the enemy lines and drew water from the spring.

**4** When they brought it to David, he considered the matter and concluded that drinking it would be to drink the blood of those who had risked their lives — so he poured it out as an offering to God and would not drink it.

**5** Thus reason proved master of desire.

**6** In the case of Joseph: that most chaste man, when the wife of Potiphar persistently invited him to satisfy her desire, checked the passion by the power of reason.

**7** For though he was a young man at the height of his passions, he subdued the craving of desire through reason.

**8** Reason proves to be sovereign not only over sexual desire but over every form of desire.

**9** The law commands: you shall not covet your neighbor's wife nor anything that belongs to your neighbor — and since the law itself orders us not to covet, I think I am all the more able to convince you that reason is sovereign over the passions.

**10** In the same way, the passions that obstruct righteousness are overcome by reason; just as the temperate mind overcomes the impulses of the body, so too it commands the passions of the soul.

**11** Why, then, does any man who lives under the whole law not overcome his passions through reason? For it is the law that gives reason authority over both soul and body.

**12** How then can any enemy of reason refuse to believe that the mind is sovereign over the passions?

**13** Moses himself, that venerable lawgiver, burned with indignation at those who rose against him, yet he kept his passion in subjection to reason and did nothing that was prompted by rage alone.

**14** He restrained his impulse, returned to his duties, and when God appeared to him he obeyed the divine command with complete composure.

**15** Such was the tempered reason of Moses. He did not smother his passion but controlled it and directed it to the service of God's will.

**16** For reason does not destroy the passions but directs them toward noble and lawful ends.

**17** It deflects anger from murder and channels it toward righteous correction; it restrains greed from robbery and turns it toward generosity; it keeps desire from adultery and directs it toward lawful love.

**18** By training the mind to be satisfied with what is necessary, reason can master even the most powerful craving.

**19** All the examples of self-denial that our ancestors performed in adherence to the law confirm this conclusion.

**20** Reason is truly sovereign over the passions, as the law itself teaches.
